summary:
Canada is among the safer large destinations for trans visitors, and Nunavut stands under that national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Federal identity documents can carry an X marker, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and no jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Nunavut layers its own statutory protection on top of that federal floor. In March 2017 Nunavut MLAs voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31, amending the territory's Human Rights Act to add gender identity and gender expression alongside sexual orientation as protected grounds. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At the time, nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws, which made Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.

Legal gender recognition is available on a declaratory basis. On 18 September 2025 Nunavut MLAs voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore a third, non-binary sex-designation option on Nunavut birth certificates through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck the provision from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill. The bill then passed third reading, and sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals.

Gender-affirming medical care is publicly funded in the territory. Nunavut's Health Department began funding transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents in March 2022, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty among the covered procedures, delivered through a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The territorial LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside Iqaluit.

National hate-crime data supplies context but no territorial breakdown. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, a 1% rise and a 169% increase over 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000 people. Incidents motivated by gender identity or gender expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and up 184% since 2020; sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, though June 2024 alone recorded 113, more than double the monthly average of roughly 50. Incident rates run about 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, and Nunavut has no metropolitan reporting hub of that kind.

Conditions inside correctional institutions are the weakest point in the record. Federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and transgender prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery; litigation has tested both placement and gender-affirming care, including the case of Synthia Kavanagh, represented by lawyer Barbara findlay. A 2022 report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. These concerns bear on a transit visitor only if detained.
tangentialFactors:
Sub-provincial policy turbulence in Canada is concentrated in schools and sport and falls mainly on minors and residents rather than visitors. Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or disclose their gender identity at school, drawing calls for repeal from human rights groups and subsequent litigation. Alberta passed its Health Statutes Amendment Act, Education Amendment Act and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them from legal challenge through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause. Nunavut has enacted none of these measures.

National sexual-minority hate-crime trends run in different directions. The 26% fall in sexual-orientation-motivated incidents in 2024 ended three consecutive years of increases off a 2023 peak of 889, while gender identity and gender expression motivations rose for a fourth straight year. Egale Canada's analysis of the same police-reported dataset supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures.

The gap between territorial commitments and delivery is widest outside the capital. Positive Space's 2022 remarks on the transition-care funding noted that residents in the communities could not readily find out what is covered and how to access it, which is the pattern a visitor or new arrival is most likely to encounter. The 2025 birth-certificate amendment passed after the standing committee had removed the non-binary option, so the measure was contested inside the legislature before it survived.
localsOnly:
Residents can invoke both the Canadian Human Rights Act and Nunavut's Human Rights Act, which has listed gender identity and gender expression as protected grounds since the unanimous 2017 passage of Bill 31, giving a territorial complaint route in addition to the federal one.

Residents may request a non-binary sex designation on a Nunavut birth certificate under the Vital Statistics Act as amended in September 2025, alongside the male and female options.

The Government of Nunavut funds transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents, including breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty, through a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. Access depends on information that Positive Space has said is lacking for people living outside the capital.

Hate-crime reporting in Nunavut sits within police-reported national statistics that do not break out territorial counts by motivation, and gender identity and gender expression motivations are recorded separately from sexual orientation in the national release.
outOfScopeNotes:
Nunavut-specific hate-crime figures by motivation are not established by the sources; the Statistics Canada release reports national totals and does not isolate the territory, so the local volume of gender-identity-motivated incidents remains unresolved.

No source in this inventory reports the operational status of the non-binary birth-certificate option after the September 2025 vote, including whether the amendment is in force and how registry offices are applying it.

Whether the transition-care partnership covers travel and accommodation costs for residents outside Iqaluit is not stated in the sources; only the funding commitment and the reported information gaps are documented.

No visitor-specific incident data exists for Nunavut: accounts of discrimination, refusal of service or harassment experienced by trans travellers in the territory are not sourced here.

The correctional findings cited concern federal institutions and, in one study, Nova Scotia; their application to Nunavut correctional facilities is not established by these sources.
